title: Find the Maximum Length of a Good Subsequence I
statement:
Call a sequence of integers **good** when, walking from its first element to its last, the value switches between neighbouring elements at most `k` times; that is, at most `k` positions `i` (with `0 <= i <= length - 2`) have `seq[i] != seq[i + 1]`.

Given the integer array `nums` and the non-negative integer `k`, return the greatest length a good subsequence of `nums` can have. A subsequence keeps some of the elements (possibly all) in their original order.
notes:
## Intuition

A good subsequence is a chain of blocks of equal values, with at most `k` switches between blocks. Trying every subsequence is exponential, but the only things that matter about a chain are where it ends and how many switches it has used. So let `dp[i][changes]` be the longest good subsequence that ends exactly at index `i` and uses at most `changes` switches.

## Approach

1. Make an `n` by `k + 1` table `dp`, and `best = 0`.
2. For each end index `i` and each budget `changes`, start at `1`: `nums[i]` alone is good.
3. Try every earlier index `prev` as the element just before `i`:
   - equal values add no switch: `dp[prev][changes] + 1`;
   - different values cost one switch, allowed only when `changes > 0`: `dp[prev][changes - 1] + 1`.
4. Keep the largest value seen in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 2, 1, 1, 3]`, `k = 2`. Rows are `dp[i][0..2]`:

- `i = 0` (1): `[1, 1, 1]`.
- `i = 1` (2): following the 1 costs a switch: `[1, 2, 2]`.
- `i = 2` (1): following index 0 is free (2); following index 1 costs a switch, so `dp[1][1] + 1 = 3` fits only budget 2: `[2, 2, 3]`.
- `i = 3` (1): following index 2 adds one at the same budget: `[3, 3, 4]`.
- `i = 4` (3): every earlier value differs, so it extends row 3 one budget lower: `[1, 4, 4]`.

`best` is `4`, for example `[1, 1, 1, 3]` (one switch) or `[1, 2, 1, 1]` (two switches). The whole array would need three switches.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · k): every `(i, changes)` pair scans all earlier indices.
- Space: O(n · k) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- The budget is "at most" `k`, so a chain using fewer switches still counts; storing exactly-`changes` values would need an extra max over budgets.
- A switch only happens between neighbouring kept elements; skipped elements cost nothing.
- Start every cell at 1, or a lone element is never counted.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[i][changes]` | longest good subsequence ending at index `i` with at most `changes` switches |
| `i` | index of the last kept element |
| `prev` | index of the element kept just before `i` |
| `changes` | the switch budget for this cell |
| `best` | longest length found anywhere |

narration.7: Fill in every switch budget from 0 up to k.
narration.8: Keeping nums[i] by itself is always a good subsequence of length 1.

narration.11: Extend the chain ending at prev with the same budget.
narration.12: Different neighbours need one switch, so the budget must be positive.
narration.13: Extend the chain ending at prev that used one switch fewer.
narration.16: Record the best length seen so far.
narration.19: Return the longest good subsequence over all end points and budgets.
